title: Grief Class 3
speaker: Reizan Bob Penny
summary: Reizan Bob Penny takes up Susan Berman's book The Five Ways We Grieve and walks through its five grieving styles: nomad, memorialist, normalizer, activist, and seeker. Each style comes with its gifts and its pitfalls, such as the widow who stays in a black dress for years, or the activist who burns out chasing a cure for cancer. Reizan shows how subtle the styles can be by describing a response to a father's death that looks like a seeker's but was really a memorialist's gesture of honoring him. After small-group sharing, Reizan names the nomad as the predominant style, recalls setting off on a bicycle trip with no plans, and wonders whether the normalizer's approach could bring some stability to finances.

sentences.text: The material is in Susan Berger's book, *The Five Ways We Grieve*.
I'd like us to get a sense of these five different grieving styles, to really get what they're all about, so that we can see where we fit into all of that.
Her model about grieving is not about a set process that most any person in a situation of grief would go through.

Rather, it's a system of personality types or styles that each person has, perhaps from their history of grief, what they've learned through what they've observed in their family related to grief, or maybe their own natural proclivity towards a particular style.
That's the way they approach their own situations of grief, and then they play it out through enacting that style however it may go.
Of course, these five different styles aren't completely rigid in terms of how they relate to us individually.
We'll probably see ourselves identified in more than one, or in pieces and parts of many.
But it's part of her theory that we would mostly, predominantly see ourselves in one particular style.
I've even started to consider whether we might have layers of these styles going on.
In other words, there's a style that we show more, or maybe one we feel more, and then a different style sort of underneath that.

Sometimes you might find that a particular gesture you enact in the grieving process has all the hallmarks of a particular style, but you're really doing that gesture not out of that style but out of a different style.
It just looks that way.

For instance, if you were here to listen to my Way-seeking mind talk, as an example, the response I had when my father died could easily be seen as the style of the seeker: someone who in response to grief would make a decision, "I'm going to pursue an attention towards issues of life and death and spiritual issues and religious issues."
But actually, I think for myself that particular gesture was more a memorialist style, because I was doing that very much in respect to what I saw of my father, in honoring him.
In a sense, I was carrying forward, in my own way, his religious convictions as a way of memorializing him.

So you see how it's kind of subtle, and you want to think a little bit about how it really is for you with these grieving styles, because it does matter in terms of understanding your grief process and how you really are approaching things.
So, the five grieving styles.
She's laid these out in somewhat of an order that has a little bit of logic.
The first style she calls the nomad.
*In the time soon after a loss, we all somewhat find ourselves in the role of the nomad.
Our shock at what we've lost temporarily leaves us unable to respond with anything other than disorientation and either intense or numb feelings.
But the style of behavior we often associate with most people initially experiencing loss continues to follow someone with a nomad grieving style onward through life.
Intense feelings and a preoccupied train of thought related to the loss continue.
Other activities, especially those requiring goal setting and planning, get pushed aside.*
*A nomad may go through life feeling unconnected to their own life, unable to realize or even identify goals, unable to create stability in work or relationships.
In essence, everything is put on hold until more healing can occur.

But since this type of person tends to not look at grief square in the face to find out what is there for him or her, the nomad goes forward with a great amount of unresolved feelings below the surface, feelings he or she may not even recognize.
Many people find their way through this period of time and come to new goals and aspirations for their lives, goals that recognize the loss they've experienced.
But the true nomad only recognizes their loss to a small degree, enough to continue functioning and going forward with life's usual demands.

But a sense of moving forward eludes them, and a continual feeling of unfulfilled energy accompanies their days, contributing to a compounding sense of guilt mapped over the grief: guilt for not accomplishing goals in their lives while at the same time feeling incapable of doing so.
A typical road for the nomad is to submerge a part of their lives in numbing activities.
Sex, drugs, and gambling would perhaps be the big three, but other activities could as easily serve.
The key about this is that these activities are ultimately unfulfilling.
They are forced substitutes for living a full life of resolved grief.
But the nomad does not recognize this fully and feels stuck in a cycle of pursuing these numbing activities.*

*Nomads may have achieved an outward appearance in their lives of stability, a family, a job, friends, and activities, but a key thing is that they themselves do not feel that they are where they want to be in their lives on some fundamental level.
They might even understand very well the strategies they employ to derail their goals, but feel locked into continuing with them.
A hidden glimmer of advantage exists for those who find themselves in this perhaps least favorable style of grieving.
The ability of the nomad to stay uncommitted and ungrounded in their lives may actually serve to give them a chance to imagine a shift to another grieving style as an accessible choice.*
The memorialist is the next grieving style.
*Probably the largest percentage of people will find themselves identifying with the style of the memorialist when faced with loss.
It's the style most universally accepted as an appropriate and standard grieving style.
Funerals and memorial services closely following the death of a loved one are the clearest examples of how the memorialist style is imbued in how most people approach loss, at least initially.
In fact, those who find funerals and memorials healing events indispensable to the full processing of loss probably do so because they feel a deeper identity with this style of grieving.*

*Those who find memorial services unnecessary, difficult, off the mark, or simply rituals to assuage the feelings of living with no meaning towards the loss itself may feel these ways because they identify more strongly with another style of grieving.
The memorialist style is intimately connected with the passage of time.

Anniversaries signify new moments of grieving and new reflections upon the continuing legacy of the loss, both for the stages of healing in the life of the griever and also for the continued example that the life of the lost one provides as an inspiration.
We see this in our most public examples of this style, such as Martin Luther King Day.
The memorialist style is connected with being public with our grieving because a memorial is often something put up to show others the importance of the person or thing that has been lost.
We are encouraged by the memorialist to always remember and to go back to this process of remembering with regularity and see how the loss changes shape over time.

At the same time, the memorialist can find equal significance in privately observing anniversaries and other gestures of personal meaning, even continuing with a favorite activity or ritual that the one we lost had in their life, as if picking up the fallen banner and carrying it forward.
Who carves the turkey now?
Who puts the star on the tree?
Who reads the bedtime story?*
*These activities are continued, but always with a conscious memory of who began them.
In these ways, the memorialist embodies in their lives the one who was lost.

The loss is reimagined within the context of time as a significant marker, a moment of transition imbued with symbolism and significance, where the life of the one lost gains a revered status and now provides continued inspiration for those who remain.
In this way, the memorialist achieves healing through transforming grief into gratitude for the life of the person or thing they have lost.
Along with the apparent advantages that this style presents come also some potential disadvantages.
The memorialist may become overly attached to the one they lost.
The widow carrying forward for years in a black dress is the classic example of this style taken to a level of detriment.

It may be that the memorialist literally fills their life with such an aura of memorial to the one lost that their own life gets squeezed out and frozen at some point in the past, in the moment of loss.*
The next healing style she discusses is the normalizer.

*The normalizer responds to loss through moving towards recreating the formerly positive attributes of life that existed before the loss, or creating new patterns of stability in response to a lack they felt before the loss.
They are widows who remarry in order to continue forward with a life of marriage that they highly valued from before the loss.
They are adult children who establish solid and full families of their own after their family of origin and experienced a major disruption in the loss of a parent or sibling.
They are family members who find reconciliation from prior estrangement after the loss of a loved one brings them back together.
And some may work towards normal and stable family and social ties after a loss exactly because they did not have those in relationship to the significant person in their lives who they lost.
And the loss has become not so much a cathartic event of tears and sadness as much as a liberating event allowing them now to have the life they always felt they lacked before.*
*A daughter may find a loving mentor to essentially fill the void always left by the lack of affection they felt from a mother who they never felt could provide the support they always wanted.

A person may establish a new, extensively connected community of friendships where in the family of origin they had they always experienced social isolation and conflict, essentially creating a new family for themselves.
And there are those who, after divorce or the loss through death of a partner, revert to discovering the identity they felt left behind as a single person.
The sense of "I" instead of "we" can be symbolized at these junctures in life most obviously by an actual change of name back to who they were called before the partnership.
These responses to loss can happen because the griever is feeling that they are honoring the wishes of the deceased: "They would have wanted me to move on."
Or because they feel freed from a situation they felt they could never change while the person who they lost was alive.
In either case, the urge is to create a renewed stability to their lives.*
*In this sense, the advantage of this healing style is that the normalizer has some clear awareness of the things they would like for their lives, and they make concrete moves to achieve these ends.
They may be some of the most satisfied of the grieving styles.
Ensconced in supportive families and satisfying careers, they may be able to say with some assuredness that they have successfully weathered their loss and built lives of security.
It may be that they are simply motivated to successfully pursue their goals in their personal lives by the recognition of mortality that the death of a loved one brings.
The disadvantages to those with this healing style are that they may tend to not notice new options available to them upon experiencing a loss.
Their drive to create normalcy and shore up the situations and conditions of their former lives may be at odds with any choice that may be available to take a new direction in life.
To move to a new place.
Experience things they did not dream of before.
Or change careers.
In the most negative manifestation, they may insist that others in their immediate family dispense with their own grieving styles and get on with things.
Their need to normalize may come through in an effort to control the entire social environment, including what is acceptable for others to feel and express.*
The next healing style she calls the activist.
The activist identity in grieving is embodied in this quote from Bertolt Brecht, used in Susan Berger's book:
*Do not fear death so much as the inadequate life.*
*The activist is concerned with social justice, with the welfare of others, or with carrying forward uncompleted work left undone by the deceased.
Of the healing styles, the activist may be the most direct and driven to do something concrete in response to the loss they have experienced.

They may establish a research foundation to explore an illness, establish a trust fund for a cause in the name of the deceased, or carry through with extensive efforts to complete a body of life work left unfinished by the one they have lost.
Being an activist may however take on a much less public tone.

It may simply be that establishing and maintaining a solid and supportive life of one's own in the wake of loss is not so much seen as a normalizing activity, as we just discussed, as it is seen as a gesture of authenticity and dedication to a sense of purpose embodied in creating a personal life path.
Activism is the style of grieving perhaps that most manifests as a total sense of purpose in life.
The activist feels compelled to devote significant energies toward their newfound activities and goals after a loss.
The line between an activist and other styles such as a memorializer should be examined for clarity.

Sierra Club Books, producing a coffee table book to the loss of Glen Canyon behind the waters of a dam, serves as memorial, but mostly essentially an activist purpose, similar to annual memorials to the lives of those who died on September 11th.
The message is: we will know intimately what it is we have lost so that this may never happen again.*
The key function of this style for healing for the bereaved person is that their lives become filled with purpose in response to their loss.
The activist stays in touch intimately with the felt sense of loss as a necessary touchstone, a reminder for why they have chosen the work they do to honor their loss.
But they transform that grief from debilitating sadness into an active life of purpose.

Activists who have motivated through loss have achieved great things in the world, from advocating for thousands of missing and abused children, to researching for the cure of terrible diseases, to championing for the rights of whole oppressed populations of people.

But the line can be drawn back also from these sorts of grand efforts for public welfare to simply the fulfillment of unrealized dreams and work left behind by the deceased: research left incomplete, a trail dreamed of but not yet built.
Therefore, again, it almost blends with the role of the memorializer.
The key difference, however, is not to primarily memorialize the person who was lost themselves, but more to carry forward their work for the benefit of many.
The pitfalls of this healing style are the same as for anyone in general doing activist work in the world: burnout.

Since the activist griever in general feels a stronger inner compulsion to fulfill their chosen work than other styles, there may be a driven quality to what they do that ignores their natural limits and personal needs.
The activist griever needs to be aware that the mandate they feel compelled to fulfill from their loss is not a goal that exists only out in the world alone.
Curing cancer may not be possible in one lifetime, and if that is the goal, then the failure of an activist's grieving process may be written in the cards from the outset.

The activist needs to always be reminded that their compulsion to do their work comes from unresolved grief, and coming to understand and heal their own grief is essential to the success of their work.
The last, the fifth healing style she mentions significantly, perhaps in a sort of a line from the nomad to now a wider style, is the seeker.

The seeker style of grieving embodies a spiritual and religious response to loss, and an awakened recognition of mortality, the mysteries of death, questions about the afterlife, or the meaning of our temporal lives.

Seekers may have a prior religious life that directs how they respond to losses, and as such may feel that their established prior grounding in a faith supports their life through all loss and gain, with a relative equanimity perhaps unavailable to those who do not have a similar grounding.
Or they may be awakened through loss into religious and spiritual understandings that they did not know they possessed.
Significantly, in Susan Berger's book, there's an extended quote from a Zen Buddhist practitioner reflecting on how Buddhism relates to this healing style.
This practitioner named Matthew, a Zen Buddhist practitioner she interviewed, says:
*One of the things I've observed throughout the years is the number of people who became famous in Buddhism after great loss.
The Zen master Dogen, founder of the Soto Zen School, which was the precursor to the San Francisco Zen Center, had both his parents die by the time he was 11.
Nakagawa Soen Roshi, a very important Zen master in the rise of Zen in America, also lost his father as a child.
Robert, who was my current teacher's teacher, didn't lose his parents but was sent away from home at the age of two and experienced great psychological trauma.
I think that one of the reasons Buddhism attracts individuals who have experienced losses is because of the Four Noble Truths.
These are the main teachings of the Dharma, the wisdom of the enlightened Buddha, that gave to the world in the 5th century BC.
The first two core teachings state that life is difficult, that we must free ourselves from the attachments to things, feelings, beliefs, and people that can obscure the reality.
All things change and we must accept the impermanence in life.
The third teaching is that there is an end to the suffering we experience in what the Buddha called Nirvana, inner peace, freedom from attachment and fulfillment.
And the fourth and final truth is that there is an eightfold path we can follow to reach this sense of peace.*
Seekers find healing through an increased awareness of the connectedness of life, of meaning in the process of life and death, and acceptance of the transitory nature of all things.
Their loss is put into context within a newly energized conception of all life.
Often they find new communities of people who share their faith and therefore can support them through the healing process in ways they never experienced in their lives before.

The pitfalls of this style of healing can come from an overshadowing aspect that belief, dogma, or established faith can have over any contradictory feelings that despite any effort the griever may still harbor.

The effort of religious mentors to advise the griever to see the loss as God's plan or to assuage sadness with assurances that the lost one is in a better place may never settle correctly, but simply serve to inform the griever that any feelings to the contrary, no matter how valid they may seem, must be put aside in the face of these religious truths.
A seeker may even provide a sense of guilt to themselves, feeling that if they were truly spiritual, if they had real faith, then why do they still feel sadness and loss?
So as we can see, each of these styles has sort of positive and then shadow sides, and in that sense it's quite possible to see how they can mesh together and be combined in some ways.

What I'd like to do now is break into small groups, and what we will do is try and see if we can identify our own history with grief and our own processes with one of these healing styles most predominantly, and talk for a while about how that is for us, how we see ourselves, examples from our life that really illustrate that, and maybe to what degree that style has or maybe hasn't been working in the way we've gone through grief in the past.
It seems to me that on this question, this class and the last class, there's been a lot to say.
Sometimes when we do these sharing times, people stretch a little bit to fill up four or five minutes, but with this topic, it seems as though people really let it run over, let the time run over.
It just seems like people have a lot to say.
Well, I want to move on to another set of sharing where we extend this question a little bit farther.

By way of going into that, and since I didn't do a sharing session just now, I thought that I would just share my own personal perspective on the question you guys were just talking about, and then lead into also the next question, which is: what other or others of the other healing styles, and the one you primarily identified with, do you imagine might be a helpful healing style for you to shift over into at times to help you more with your grieving process than the style you predominantly, habitually use?
For me, I would have to say in response to that question you were just talking about that my predominant healing style has been the nomad.
When I think about my life as an inner-felt thing, I don't feel particularly stable and normalized.
I don't feel as though activism that I do in the world is in much response to the losses I've felt, but I do feel a sense of unrealized goals and ungroundedness.
So I would say that basically based off of that, it's somewhat surprising to me, but then in studying this book I actually came to that understanding.

I did feel as though her depiction of the nomad was highly negative and only had a few glimmers of positivity associated with it, and I can really see the truth in that now to some degree, as I even look at my own life, of strategies to keep myself ungrounded, or habitual.

At the same time, and perhaps it has a lot to do with the other styles I tend to blend in there at the sides, seeker and memorializer, my nomad personality at times I feel has had a sort of a purest expression.
In other words, an ability to really let go of whatever it was I thought, or whatever direction I thought my life might be going into, in accepting anything new that came my way.

And I think most pointedly that story from my life about heading off on a bicycle trip, literally, quite literally, had exactly no plans for the rest of my life, and didn't even know where I was going, was to me a very liberating experience.
It's one that I realize is very difficult for most other people to duplicate, or even for me to duplicate at a different point in time in my life.
Just imagine, you don't have any place to live, you don't have a job, you aren't thinking about a particular career of any type, you don't have anybody, and where are you going?
That's pretty open.
And I found that really amazing things happened to me through that process.
But like I said, that's sort of a purest expression of that nomad style, but everything about the nomad, the negative aspects, come along with it.
So I would say that these other styles, especially the seeker, really manifested in my Buddhist practice.
And memorializer, which is not something I've done a lot of, but every time I have, it's felt really healing and significant, and probably something I should do more of.
These have been things that have essentially shored up that crazy nomad from just becoming a hermit up in the hills, just not being a social person at all.
So that really brings up to me the idea that perhaps I should explore those other styles deeply.
Of course the seeker I've probably explored about as deep as I can imagine; I'm certainly gaining benefit in that role.
But perhaps the normalizer is something I should really be looking at, really looking at the stability that my nomad personality is really depriving me of.
I do try and look at that with my finances and whatnot, but it's been a somewhat unfocused attempt so far.
And until reading this book, I didn't realize there was sort of a framework to put that attempt into.
Rather than like a self-improvement program, like I'll try and do this one thing to make things better, but I'm still actually doing that from my basic perspective as a nomad.
Nomads aren't any good at that.
They aren't good at normalizing.
So obviously I'm always failing there.
So maybe I need to actually look at what this normalizer style really is and the full picture of it and see if I can try and put myself in those shoes a little bit.

So anyway, that's sort of a combination of me addressing both the question that we were just talking about and then also this next question, which is: which of the other healing styles, one style or combination of the other styles, would be really good for you to explore to help fill in the gaps that your predominant healing style seems to be leaving you with?

Of the healing styles, the activist may be the most direct and driven to do something concrete in response to the loss they have experienced.

They may establish a research foundation to explore an illness, establish a trust fund for a cause in the name of the deceased, or carry through with extensive efforts to complete a body of life work left unfinished by the one they have lost. Being an activist may however take on a much less public tone. It may simply be that establishing and maintaining a solid and supportive life of one's own in the wake of loss is not so much seen as a normalizing activity, as we just discussed, as it is seen as a gesture of authenticity and dedication to a sense of purpose embodied in creating a personal life path. Activism is the style of grieving perhaps that most manifests as a total sense of purpose in life. The activist feels compelled to devote significant energies toward their newfound activities and goals after a loss. The line between an activist and other styles such as a memorializer should be examined for clarity. Sierra Club Books, producing a coffee table book to the loss of Glen Canyon behind the waters of a dam, serves as memorial, but mostly essentially an activist purpose, similar to annual memorials to the lives of those who died on September 11th. The message is we will know intimately what it is we have lost so that this may never happen again.

The key function of this style for healing for the bereaved person is that their lives become filled with purpose in response to their loss. The activist stays in touch intimately with the felt sense of loss as a necessary touchstone, a reminder for why they have chosen the work they do to honor their loss. But they transform that grief from debilitating sadness into an active life of purpose. Activists who have motivated through loss have achieved great things in the world, from advocating for thousands of missing and abused children, to researching for the cure of terrible diseases, to championing for the rights of whole oppressed populations of people. But the line can be drawn back also from these sorts of grand efforts for public welfare to simply the fulfillment of unrealized dreams and work left behind by the deceased, research left incomplete, a trail dreamed of but not yet built, and therefore again almost blend with the role of the memorializer. The key difference, however, is not to primarily memorialize the person who was lost themselves, but more to carry forward their work for the benefit of many. The pitfalls of this healing style are the same as for anyone in general doing activist work in the world, burnout. And since the activist griever in general feels a stronger inner compulsion to fulfill their chosen work than other styles, there may be a driven quality to what they do that ignores their natural limits and personal needs.

The activist griever needs to be aware that the mandate they feel compelled to fulfill from their loss is not a goal that exists only out in the world alone. Curing cancer may not be possible in one lifetime, and if that is the goal, then the failure of an activist's grieving process may be written in the cards from the outset. The activist needs to always be reminded that their compulsion to do their work comes from unresolved grief, and coming to understand and heal their own grief is essential to the success of their work.
